item.title: Cannabis use Disclosure and Opioid Prescribing at Emergency Department Discharge
item.description:
Background: It is unclear whether documented cannabis use disclosure is independently associated with opioid prescribing practices when patients discharge from the emergency department (ED).

Objective: To examine associations between cannabis use disclosure and opioid prescribing as well as dose among adults with selected acute painful conditions.

Methods: We conducted a retrospective observational study of adult patients seen in the ED between 2021 and 2023 in a Southern California healthcare system. For patients with multiple ED visits, only the earliest encounter was included in the study. Eligible conditions included major/long-bone fractures, acute low-back/lumbar/sciatic conditions, and selected minor acute musculoskeletal injuries. The primary outcome was an opioid prescription at discharge. Among who were prescribed an opioid, secondary outcomes were total and daily prescribed morphine milligram equivalents (MME). Multivariable models adjusted for demographic, clinical, substance-use, utilization, year, and diagnosis variables.

Results: Among 3159 patients, 507 (16.0%) disclosed cannabis use. Opioids were prescribed to 27.6% of cannabis-disclosing and 31.3% of documented noncannabis patients (absolute difference, -3.6 percentage points; 95% CI, -7.9 to 0.6). Cannabis disclosure was not associated with discharge opioid prescribing after adjusting for covariates (adjusted odds ratio, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.67-1.11). Among opioid recipients, cannabis disclosure was not associated with total MME (adjusted mean ratio, 1.11; 95% CI, 0.92-1.34) or daily MME (1.07; 95% CI, 0.95-1.21).

Conclusions: Documented cannabis disclosure was not independently associated with opioid prescribing at ED discharge or prescribed opioid dose.

Clobes TA, Kraybill M, Himebaugh S, Jones B, Jaskolka M

item.title: Cardioversion of Stable Atrial Fibrillation in the Emergency Department: Electrical Versus Pharmacological in the Era of Overcrowding
item.description:
Background: Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a leading cause of emergency department (ED) visits. Optimizing the management of recent-onset AF is crucial to reduce length of stay (LOS) and improve ED resource utilization.

Study objectives: To evaluate differences in ED LOS between pharmacological (PC) and electrical cardioversion (ECV) in patients with recent-onset AF. Secondarily, to compare adverse event profiles of propofol versus midazolam.

Methods: This retrospective, single-center observational study analyzed ED patients with stable recent-onset AF who underwent PC or ECV. Patients with hemodynamic instability, combined sedatives, or concurrent clinical issues prolonging ED LOS were excluded from the primary analysis.

Results: A total of 575 patients were analyzed: ECV-propofol (n = 201), ECV-midazolam (n = 27), flecainide (n = 312), propafenone (n = 15), and amiodarone (n = 20). The overall ECV approach demonstrated a significantly shorter median LOS (114 min) compared with overall PC (130 min) (p = 0.006). In a propensity score matched analysis (excluding crossover pathways), ECV-propofol showed a numerically shorter LOS (106 min) versus flecainide (118 min), though not statistically significant (p = 0.086). However, a secondary analysis of 121 crossover patients revealed that pharmacological failures drove massive ED delays (median LOS 317 min). Adverse events in the ECV-propofol cohort (5%) were strictly minor and self-limited.

Conclusion: While uncomplicated PC with flecainide approaches the temporal efficiency of propofol sedation, the overall ECV strategy is associated with a significantly shorter ED LOS. By adopting structured propofol-based ECV protocols, emergency physicians can effectively avoid the enormous time delays that occur when initial pharmacological interventions fail.

Mariani A, Geniere Nigra S, Lorenzi L, Battaglini C, Francesconi R

item.title: Multimodal Nonopioid Analgesia Versus Opioid-First Approaches for Acute Pain in the Emergency Department: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials
item.description:
Background: The opioid crisis has prompted emergency departments (EDs) to adopt multimodal, opioid-sparing analgesia for acute pain; however, comparative effectiveness and safety vs. opioid-first approaches remain incompletely characterized across common ED presentations.

Objective: To evaluate whether multimodal nonopioid or opioid-sparing analgesic strategies provide analgesia comparable or superior to opioid-first regimens for adults presenting to EDs with acute pain. Safety (opioid exposure and treatment-related adverse events) was assessed as a secondary aim.

Methods: Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from 2010 to 2026 in PubMed/MEDLINE and Embase enrolling adults (≥18 years) with acute pain from renal colic, trauma/musculoskeletal injury, or primary headache (migraine, tension-type, or cluster) treated in hospital-based EDs. Eligible interventions compared multimodal or opioid-sparing regimens with opioid-only or opioid-dominant regimens. Risk of bias was assessed using Cochrane RoB 2.

Results: Seventeen RCTs (n = 7288) were included. Evidence was unevenly distributed, as 13 trials (76%; n = 5248) evaluated musculoskeletal trauma. Ibuprofen-acetaminophen achieved pain relief comparable to opioid-acetaminophen combinations for musculoskeletal pain. For migraine, prochlorperazine-diphenhydramine outperformed hydromorphone, with 86% achieving mild or no headache at 1 h vs. 52%. For renal colic, intramuscular diclofenac and intravenous paracetamol provided analgesia equivalent or superior to morphine with lower adverse event rates.

Conclusion: Multimodal nonopioid and opioid-sparing strategies generally provided comparable or superior analgesia to opioid-first regimens while reducing opioid exposure and adverse events, aligning with current guidelines. Because these conditions differ clinically and evidence was uneven and synthesized descriptively, the findings should be interpreted by condition rather than cumulatively.

Chijioke W, Troche L, Ojukwu K, Kunjappy M

item.title: Are Muscle Relaxants an Effective Treatment for Patients With Acute Low Back Pain?
item.description:
Background: Acute low back pain (LBP) is a common condition evaluated and managed in the healthcare setting. While numerous treatment options exist, the efficacy varies, and it is important to balance the benefits with the risk of harm. Muscle relaxants are commonly prescribed in practice, yet it is important to understand the effectiveness to inform their continued use.

Clinical question: Are muscle relaxants an effective treatment for patients with acute low back pain?

Evidence review: Studies retrieved included four randomized controlled trials and two meta-analyses. These studies provide estimates of the effectiveness and safety of muscle relaxants in patients with acute LBP. The data found muscle relaxants do not improve symptom resolution or function in emergency department (ED) patients with acute LBP.

Conclusion: Based upon the available literature, muscle relaxants are not associated with improved outcomes for acute LBP and should not be routinely prescribed in the ED setting.

Long B, Keim SM, Gottlieb M, Edwards C, Farrell SE
